title: Type Assertions and `as`
description: Learn to tell TypeScript what type a value really is using assertions, `as`, and `satisfies`.

data.text: Sometimes TypeScript knows less about a value than you do. Type assertions let you tell the compiler to trust your judgment, without changing the runtime value.

data.title: Type Assertion with as
Two Assertion Styles
Assertions Do Not Convert
data.text: A type assertion is a compile-time instruction only. It does not change the value or perform any runtime conversion. Use it only when you have verified the type yourself.
The `as const` assertion tells TypeScript to treat a value as an immutable, literal type.

data.title: Const Assertion

data.text: The `satisfies` keyword checks that a value matches a type while preserving its original literal types. It is safer than `as` because it errors when the check fails.

data.title: satisfies
data.content: Checking a value against a type

rows: Trusted casts from unknown or DOM
Checking a value against a shape

data.title: Prefer `satisfies`
data.text: Whenever you only need to check that a value matches a shape, use `satisfies` instead of `as`. It keeps literal types intact and fails loudly when the shape changes.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `as const` to freeze literal types
data.takeaway: Type assertions bridge the gap between what TypeScript knows and what you know.
